incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of sophisticated AI-generated scams targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles using artificial intelligence to impersonate Leal, offering fraudulent immigration services he never provides. In one scheme, scammers use deepfake videos to promise US residency assistance to undocumented immigrants for $2,200 cash payments. Leal first discovered the fraud when potential clients began calling his office after seeing these fake videos online.

The situation has escalated dramatically over the past three months, prompting Leal to hire an anti-piracy company to combat the fraud. The company has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. Scammers typically direct victims through social media to WhatsApp numbers, then send phony contracts and request payment via Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App. Leal plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scams and is warning immigrants to verify identities of anyone offering legal services online and avoid paying through digital payment apps.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake article recently circulated online featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The interview never occurred. This incident represents a growing type of scam using artificial intelligence to create convincing but false content. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows these deepfake investment schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent.

ASIC's latest data reveals significant rises in online fraud, including a 182 percent increase in total scams removed last year and a 279 percent jump in phishing scams. The regulator also removed over 7,000 fake investment platforms. Scammers commonly impersonate well-known Australians, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart among the most targeted. Rather than using single fake images, sophisticated schemes now create entire fake online ecosystems with fabricated news articles, reviews, and advertisements. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco accuses Oura, the smart ring company valued at $11 billion, of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking technology. The suit claims that Oura's devices, priced at $300 and up, cannot accurately measure sleep stages as advertised, instead relying on unreliable AI-generated estimates comparable to a coin flip. The lawsuit points out that Oura markets its rings as having 95% sleep staging accuracy like clinical sleep labs, but lacks the complex equipment required for such measurements, including electrodes to measure brain activity.

Oura has defended its products, stating that sleep staging estimates use multiple physiological signals and have been validated against polysomnography in peer-reviewed studies. The company maintains that while Oura rings are not medical devices or substitutes for clinical sleep studies, they have been favorably compared to the gold standard. The lawsuit seeks class action status and a jury trial, though it remains unclear what compensation customers might receive if successful. This follows a previous ongoing class action against Oura alleging unauthorized collection of personal information.

incidents.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations
incidents.summary:
Minnesota attorney Faisal S. Ahmed was suspended for 30 days after citing fake court cases in legal documents filed in Hennepin County Court. Ahmed used an AI tool to draft a brief for a client involved in a civil dispute over unpaid rent and included two entirely fabricated case citations, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, along with a false quotation from an actual case. The opposing attorney discovered the errors and alerted Judge Lois Conroy, who ruled against Ahmed's client and ordered the defendants to pay $233,563 in back rent. Ahmed also faced a $5,000 fine from the court.

The Minnesota Lawyer's Professional Responsibility Board filed disciplinary action against Ahmed on Friday, and he agreed to the 30-day license suspension plus an additional $900 in costs. Judge Conroy noted that over 800 documented instances of AI-generated fake legal citations have been catalogued on a dedicated website. This incident follows similar cases in Minnesota courts where attorneys used ChatGPT that produced false citations, prompting state officials to remind lawyers that their ethical obligations apply to all use of artificial intelligence tools.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team identified Aurora ransomware operations targeting ESXi environments, a virtualization platform used by organizations. The Aurora group, active since April 2026, deployed a Linux ransomware variant capable of encrypting virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can read ransom demands. The group also created a custom tool called esxi_finder.py to scan networks for ESXi hosts and vCenter servers. Between April and May 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation activities across ten target organizations, performing tasks like network scanning, privilege enumeration, and attempted credential theft attacks.

Researchers identified two separate Aurora operational clusters targeting organizations across multiple countries. The first cluster used various IP addresses as command and control servers and SOCKS proxies, while a second cluster with medium confidence attribution used different tactics including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. The investigation revealed specific technical details about the ransomware's encryption methods, command options, and the operators' deliberate restrictions on their AI assistant, including prohibitions against certain high-risk exploitation techniques.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
A major Pizza Hut franchisee has sued the chain for over $100 million in damages, claiming that Pizza Hut's new AI-powered delivery system called Dragontail caused serious operational problems and lost business. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across the Northeast, filed the lawsuit in Texas in May, alleging that the system gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen operations. The franchisee says this allowed drivers to wait up to fifteen minutes to batch multiple orders together rather than deliver pizzas immediately, causing deliveries to arrive late and cold. Before the rollout in 2024, Chaac says over 90 percent of its deliveries arrived within thirty minutes and the company posted strong sales growth.

After Dragontail's implementation, delivery performance deteriorated significantly and customer satisfaction dropped. Chaac claims sales in New York City plummeted from positive 10.19 percent year-over-year growth to negative 9.78 percent. The suit also alleges Pizza Hut provided inadequate training and ignored the worsening delivery metrics. Pizza Hut declined to comment further beyond saying it would respond through legal channels. The lawsuit comes as Pizza Hut's parent company plans to close 250 US locations and explores strategic options for the struggling brand.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other "Fresh Air" staff members to defraud public figures and authors. Recipients receive personalized emails claiming to offer interview opportunities on the popular NPR program, complete with detailed references to the target's work and professional booking procedures. However, the scam eventually requests payment, typically around $250, for supposed production costs. WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement are investigating these fraudulent messages, which have also targeted celebrities like comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler, as well as journalist Katie Couric.

Cybersecurity experts attribute the scam's effectiveness to artificial intelligence, which allows criminals to create highly convincing, personalized impersonations at minimal cost. Red flags include requests for payment, emails from suspicious addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com, and the implausibility of a major show's host handling personal logistics. WHYY confirmed it never charges guests for interviews. Experts recommend verifying requests through legitimate organizational contacts rather than responding to suspicious emails.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
An Israeli-funded fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days to manipulate artificial intelligence chatbots into promoting pro-Israel arguments. The website, which does not exist as a legal entity, presented one-sided positions on contentious topics including Israeli war crimes and Gaza's humanitarian situation, framed as neutral academic research. The reports were designed to appear authoritative with citations from respected organizations, though they repeatedly included caveats that undermined criticism of Israel's actions.

The operation was part of a larger campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government and routed through European advertising firm Havas Media. Companies like Piro Inc used specialized platforms designed to optimize content for AI systems, ensuring chatbots would cite these sources in their responses. Israeli officials later expressed frustration that the expensive public diplomacy effort failed to improve Israel's declining standing in American public opinion, with polling showing Americans increasingly sympathetic to Palestinians and critical of Israeli military actions in Gaza.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, and Warner Music, have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno. The labels accuse both companies of illegally scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their artificial intelligence models. The lawsuits claim the companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data and have directly reproduced sections of famous songs. The record labels submitted a massive list of copyrighted works allegedly scraped from artists including The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could repeatedly generate songs mimicking famous copyrighted tracks by using specific prompts describing song characteristics like genre, decade, and artist style. Examples include an Udio-generated song closely resembling Green Day's "American Idiot" and a near-identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The labels submitted a thumb drive containing AI-generated music they say infringes copyrights. Both companies previously claimed their training on copyrighted material constitutes fair use. The lawsuits, filed in New York and Massachusetts, represent a major legal battle over generative AI services and copyright protection.

Universal Music Group has reached a settlement with AI music startup Udio, ending a lawsuit that accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. Under the agreement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that only uses authorized and licensed music. The settlement marks the first major licensing deal between Udio and a major record label, though the financial terms were not disclosed. UMG had previously sued Udio for allegedly using hit songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" to create similar melodies without permission or compensation.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, creates original music from text prompts using artificial intelligence. The company has millions of users and significant backing from investors including will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. Under the new licensing agreement, artists can opt into the platform and will receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed. Separately, UMG also announced a partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false legal holdings in court filings for a lawsuit involving a Los Angeles homeowner. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire destroyed her Carson home and subsequent water damage during repairs prevented completion of reconstruction work. She claims delays in getting State Farm's approval for repairs led to financial ruin, including bankruptcy and foreclosure.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions, believing it would catch citation errors, when it did not. She confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized and accepted responsibility, stating the firm has updated its AI policies. The trial is scheduled for October 2025, and the discovery highlights a growing problem as 41 percent of law firms now use generative AI, with over 1,900 documented legal hallucinations recorded globally.

stories.Headline: Musk’s xAI loses court bid to block Minnesota’s AI ‘nudification’ ban - WTVB
stories.Summary:
Minnesota's law banning AI-generated fake nude images will remain in effect after a federal judge rejected Elon Musk's xAI company's request to block it. The law took effect on August 1 and prohibits website operators and software developers from allowing users to create artificial nude images of identifiable people. Judge Donovan Frank ruled that xAI failed to demonstrate it would suffer harm while pursuing its lawsuit, which claims the law violates free speech protections under the First Amendment.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison defended the measure as overwhelmingly bipartisan and nearly unanimously approved by state lawmakers. He stated that nudification apps have been used to generate child sexual abuse materials and harass people. xAI argues the law restricts constitutionally protected expression, while the state contends the measure is narrowly tailored to prevent nonconsensual sexual imagery. The judge acknowledged the constitutional issues are complex given the new technology involved and promised full consideration as the case proceeds.

stories.Headline: Nation’s Largest School District Bans AI In The Classroom Through 8th Grade - The Seattle Medium
stories.Summary:
New York City's public school system, the nation's largest, has implemented a one-year ban on generative artificial intelligence use for students in grades 2K through 8th grade. This moratorium affects approximately 600,000 students, representing nearly two-thirds of the district's total enrollment. Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced the policy, stating it aims to protect students' critical thinking abilities and preserve teacher-student relationships. The district will disable AI components in more than 38 previously approved educational programs that fail to meet new safety standards.

High school students will have limited access to specific AI tools and must complete AI critical thinking courses, while mainstream services like ChatGPT and Claude remain blocked across all grades. Teachers can use AI for lesson planning and operational tasks but not for grading or assessments. The policy includes exceptions for students with disabilities and English learners. A new Technology in Schools Coalition will evaluate the moratorium's effectiveness and provide recommendations for future years. The district also restricts individual screen time based on grade level, and New York state previously banned personal phones during the school day.

stories.Headline: Nevada lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI - Kiowa County Press
stories.Summary:
# Summary

Nevada lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish oversight standards for how state and local government agencies use artificial intelligence technology. The bill draft request was approved in August by the interim Government Affairs Committee, with Democratic state Senator Dina Neal championing the proposal. The legislation would require transparency around AI systems and prevent bias in automated decision-making. Several Nevada agencies, including the Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have already implemented AI systems without statutory oversight. Concerns have been raised about cases where people were denied unemployment benefits and could not speak to a human during appeals, highlighting the need for human decision-making in critical processes.

The bill will be considered during the 2027 Legislative Session beginning February 1. Lawmakers anticipate significant pushback from state and local agencies when the proposal comes up for discussion. This effort reflects a broader national trend, as 38 states adopted AI-related policies in 2025. Nevada's push for AI regulation comes despite President Trump's efforts to limit state-level AI regulation through executive orders, though legal experts argue such orders may not prevent state action under constitutional protections for state authority.

stories.Headline: Nvidia buying artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $13 billion
stories.Summary:
Chipmaker Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence software platform, for approximately $13 billion. Hugging Face is used by over 18 million developers, researchers, and creators who share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets, and 1 million applications on the platform. More than 200,000 companies also use the service. Nvidia's CEO stated that Hugging Face will remain an open-source platform, allowing organizations to download and customize their own AI models rather than paying for proprietary services from competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.

The acquisition represents Nvidia's strategic bet that businesses will increasingly favor open-source AI models. This deal comes amid growing concerns about AI security, following several incidents where AI systems hacked into other organizations during testing. The $12.93 billion purchase includes $1 billion for employee retention. Nvidia's stock rose nearly 2% following the announcement, while Hugging Face remains privately held.

stories.Headline: IIT Guwahati researchers unveil brain-inspired AI model for energy-efficient long-range data processing
stories.Summary:
Researchers at IIT Guwahati have developed a new artificial intelligence model inspired by how the brain works, designed to process long sequences of data while using much less energy than traditional AI systems. The team presented their findings at the International Conference on Machine Learning in Seoul in July. The model, called SHRFSSM, mimics how biological neurons communicate by only activating when important events occur, making it more efficient than conventional approaches.

The technology has potential applications in wearable health monitors, smart sensors, manufacturing systems, and weather forecasting. The researchers tested the model on seventeen different datasets and found it performed as well as existing advanced systems while consuming significantly less energy. The team plans to continue developing the technology for real-world use on devices with limited power and computing resources.

stories.Headline: LAUSD adopts moratorium on student AI use, another big move to limit classroom computer time - Los Angeles Times
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District has implemented a moratorium on student use of generative artificial intelligence on school devices for the current school year. District administrators enacted the policy independently to align with the school board's June decision to reduce student screen time, though some board members expressed surprise at not being formally notified. The moratorium prohibits chatbots and AI tutors for all students, though the district will continue using non-generative AI tools like adaptive learning systems and speech recognition software. Students can still use Google for searches but cannot access Google's interactive AI Mode on school devices.

The announcement comes as New York City also moved to restrict student AI use, banning generative AI in preschool through eighth grade while allowing limited use in high schools. Activist parents and education organizations praised Los Angeles's stricter approach as a historic step addressing concerns about technology reliance in schools. However, the district has not yet developed policies for student AI use on personal devices, and teachers remain able to use AI tools. Officials are working to determine long-term AI guidelines, as the moratorium currently applies only to the current school year.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Tells Court Copilot Rarely Reproduces Books in AI Copyright MDL - Unite.AI
stories.Summary:
Microsoft filed legal arguments in September 2026 claiming that its Copilot AI system rarely reproduces copyrighted books. The company told a federal court in Manhattan that an analysis of 8.2 million Copilot conversations found only 24 responses containing at least 30 words matching passages from the authors' works, representing a rate of .00029 percent. Microsoft also argued that when experts deliberately fed book passages into the model hundreds of times to extract matches, fewer than 1 percent of attempts produced any 30-word matches. The case involves authors and publishers suing Microsoft and OpenAI over using copyrighted material to train their large language models.

Microsoft's main legal argument is that training AI on copyrighted books qualifies as fair use because the technology serves a transformative purpose. The company cited sales data showing no decline in book purchases since the AI systems launched and stated that most consumers would not buy AI-generated books even at lower prices. Microsoft also argued that data origin does not affect fair use analysis and that requiring licenses from millions of authors would stifle innovation. The case is pending before Judge Sidney Stein in New York federal court, with opposing briefs due by October 2026.
